cards.explanation: The answer is that nobody can say it all. The writer asks, "Who can describe the mighty acts of the LORD or fully proclaim His praise?" and the answer hangs in the air: nobody gets it all. It's like trying to count every crumb in the Dorinverse. You'll be at it forever, friends, and you'll still be praising.

The answer is True. The writer asks the LORD to visit him with His salvation "…that I may see the prosperity of Your chosen ones, and rejoice in the gladness of Your nation…" Notice it's not a solo party. He wants to be in the middle of the celebration with everyone else. A bakery is no fun with one cookie, friends.

The answer is False. They did not remember. The psalm says, "Our fathers in Egypt did not grasp Your wonders or remember Your abundant kindness; but they rebelled by the sea, there at the Red Sea." They saw wonders up close and still didn't grasp them. I've hopped into a room and forgotten why, but this is a whole other level.

The answer is by the Red Sea. The psalm says they "…rebelled by the sea, there at the Red Sea." It happens right at the water, and the writer admits it plainly. I think that honesty is what makes the rescue after it so big, friends.
The answer is power. The psalm says, "Yet He saved them for the sake of His name, to make His power known." They rebelled and He saved them anyway. That tells you something about who He is, friends.

The answer is False. Not one of the enemy made it out. The psalm says, "The waters covered their foes; not one of them remained." God saved Israel from the hand that hated them, and none of those foes remained. It's a heavy scene, so I'll just say it plainly.

The answer is that they believe and sing His praise. The psalm says, "Then they believed His promises and sang His praise." Right after the rescue, they sing. I like a good happy moment, friends, and I'm glad the psalm gives them one before things turn.
The answer is tested. The psalm says they "…craved intensely in the wilderness and tested God in the desert." Craving and testing, both in one verse. I think that's a hard one to sit with, friends.
The answer is a wasting disease. The psalm says, "So He granted their request, but sent a wasting disease upon them." They got what they asked for, and something came with it. A heavy verse, friends.

The answer is Moses and Aaron. The psalm says, "In the camp they envied Moses, as well as Aaron, the holy one of the LORD." Moses was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), and Aaron is called the holy one of the LORD. Those are the two the camp envied.

The answer is False. Dathan does not get away. The psalm says, "The earth opened up and swallowed Dathan; it covered the assembly of Abiram." The earth swallowed him, so he did not escape. I think this one is meant to make us pause, friends.

The answer is a calf. The psalm says, "At Horeb they made a calf and worshiped a molten image." They made it, and then they worshiped it. That's a lot of trust to put in something they had just made, friends.
The answer is forgot. The psalm says, "They forgot God their Savior, who did great things in Egypt…" They forgot the very One who did those great things. That's a sad thing to read, friends.

The answer is Moses, His chosen one. The psalm says God would have destroyed them "…had not Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath from destroying them." Moses, who was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), stood in the gap. I think that's a whole lot of courage, friends.

The answer is False. The psalm says, "They despised the pleasant land; they did not believe His promise." They despised the land and did not believe what God promised. That's the whole problem in one verse, friends.

The answer is that He swears to cast them down in the wilderness. The psalm says, "So He raised His hand and swore to cast them down in the wilderness…" He took an oath over their grumbling. It's a serious moment, friends, and the psalm tells it that way.

The answer is lifeless gods. The psalm says they "…yoked themselves to Baal of Peor and ate sacrifices offered to lifeless gods." Lifeless. Nothing there to hear them. I'd say that's as sad as it gets, friends.

The answer is True. The psalm says, "But Phinehas stood and intervened, and the plague was restrained." I like how plain it is. He stood, he stepped in, and the psalm says the plague was restrained, friends.

The answer is righteousness. The psalm says, "It was credited to him as righteousness for endless generations to come." That's a long stretch of credit. I'd settle for a few weeks of good reviews on my cookies, friends.

The answer is that Moses speaks rashly. The psalm says, "For they rebelled against His Spirit, and Moses spoke rashly with his lips." Even Moses, who was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), had a moment with his words. Every one of us has said something and wished it back, friends, and I think I've said it to a mixing bowl.

The answer is that they mingle and adopt their customs. The psalm says, "…but they mingled with the nations and adopted their customs." They blended in with the very peoples the LORD had commanded them to destroy. It's like adding too many ingredients until you can't find the recipe anymore, friends.
The answer is snare. The psalm says, "They worshiped their idols, which became a snare to them." A snare is a trap. They walked right into it, friends.

The answer is False. His anger did burn. The psalm says, "So the anger of the LORD burned against His people, and He abhorred His own inheritance." The psalm doesn't pretend that sin is small. I think it's why the mercy that comes later hits so hard, friends.

The answer is those who hated them. The psalm says, "He delivered them into the hand of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them." The ones who hated them ended up in charge. It's a hard verse, friends.

The answer is that He hears their cry. The psalm says, "Nevertheless He heard their cry; He took note of their distress." After all of that, He still listens. Hold on to that word, friends: nevertheless.

The answer is His covenant with them. The psalm says, "And He remembered His covenant with them, and relented by the abundance of His loving devotion." It's His covenant, not their record. That's a good thing for anyone who's had a rough season, friends.
The answer is True. The psalm says, "He made them objects of compassion to all who held them captive." Even among captors, compassion came toward them. I think that's a tender thing to read, friends.

The answer is so they can give thanks to His name. The psalm says, "Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from the nations, that we may give thanks to Your holy name, that we may glory in Your praise." The prayer ends up back at thanks, right where the psalm began (Psalm 106:1). That's a nice loop to notice, friends.
